world.summary: Some babies who died at the Countess of Chester Hospital could have been saved had the hospital notified police earlier of doctors’ suspicions that Lucy Letby was a killer, a public inquiry has concluded.1 As well as identifying a raft of failures at the hospital trust, the report recommended using digital devices to restrict access of insulin only to authorised people, installing baby monitors in all cots and incubators in neonatal units, and a system barring NHS managers dismissed for serious misconduct from moving to other NHS roles. Led by the appeal court judge Lady Justice Thirlwall, the inquiry found that hospital staff were unaware that the SUDIC (Sudden Unexpected Death in Infancy and Childhood) protocol applied to babies who never left hospital, not just those who died at home. Letby is currently serving life imprisonment after being found guilty of murdering seven babies and attempting to kill seven others from June 2015 to June 2016.2 Unexplained deaths of newborns are rare and, had the protocol been followed, police would have been called after the death of Baby A in June 2015, the report found.

world.summary: Background Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) is common in extremely preterm infants, yet optimal management—particularly the role of surgical ligation—remains controversial, with limited data on long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. This study evaluated whether a shift from an active to a restrictive surgical PDA strategy affected (1) the composite outcome of moderate-to-severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD) or death before discharge, and (2) moderate-to-severe neurodevelopmental impairment (NDI) at 2–2.5 years’ corrected age.Methods This retrospective single-center cohort study included 193 infants born at 22+0–25+6 weeks’ gestation. We compared an active surgical strategy (2014–2016, n=89) with a restrictive strategy (2018–2020, n=104).

At a time when countries are seeking new solutions to reduce the growing burden of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) – which kill more than 43 million people every year – and accelerate progress towards universal health coverage (UHC), this represents one of the largest evidence gaps in global health. Addressing this gap, the World Health Organization (WHO) today launched the WHO Global research priorities and agenda for traditional, complementary and integrative medicine 2025–2034, a landmark roadmap identifying where traditional medicine research can make the greatest contribution to improving health outcomes, addressing NCDs and advancing UHC.Governments have already committed At the Second WHO Global Summit on Traditional Medicine, held in New Delhi in December 2025, 27 Member States made formal, time-bound commitments to advance traditional medicine research.
